definition: A pair $G=(V,E)$ of a set of vertices $V$ and a set of edges $E$, where each edge joins two vertices.
In a directed graph each edge $(u,v)$ has a direction (from $u$ to $v$); in an undirected graph the edges are unordered pairs $\{u,v\}$.
The number of edges incident to a vertex. In a directed graph a vertex has an in-degree (entering edges) and an out-degree (leaving edges).
A sequence of vertices $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge. In a simple path all the vertices are distinct.
Like a path, but it may pass through the same vertices and the same edges more than once.
A path that starts and ends at the same vertex. In a simple cycle all the vertices are distinct (apart from the shared endpoint).
An undirected graph in which there is a path between every pair of vertices.
A maximal set of mutually reachable vertices. An undirected graph splits into one or more connected components.
A directed graph in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex — a directed path exists in both directions for every pair.
A maximal set of vertices of a directed graph that are pairwise mutually reachable. Every two vertices of an SCC lie on a common directed cycle.
An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. An edge is a bridge **exactly when it lies on no cycle**.
A connected, acyclic undirected graph. A tree on $n$ vertices has exactly $n-1$ edges.
An acyclic undirected graph; equivalently, a disjoint union of trees.
A subgraph of a connected graph that is a tree and includes all of the graph's vertices.
Among all spanning trees of a weighted connected graph, one whose total edge weight is smallest. With distinct weights it is unique.
In a directed graph, a vertex from which there is a directed path to every other vertex.
A directed acyclic graph with a single root of in-degree $0$, in which every other vertex has in-degree $1$.
The tree(s) formed by the edges DFS uses to discover new vertices. The remaining edges are classified as back, forward, or cross edges; an undirected DFS produces only tree and back edges.
The length — number of edges, or sum of weights — of a shortest path between two vertices; $\infty$ if no path exists.
A path between two vertices whose total weight (or, when unweighted, edge count) is the smallest possible.
The largest distance between any pair of vertices in the graph: $\max_{u,v} d(u,v)$.
A graph whose vertices split into two sets $A,B$ so that every edge joins a vertex of $A$ to a vertex of $B$. Equivalently, a graph with no odd-length cycle.
An undirected graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge.
A subset of vertices in which every two vertices are adjacent — a complete subgraph.
A directed graph that contains no directed cycle. These are exactly the graphs that admit a topological ordering.
A graph in which every vertex has the same degree $r$.
A linear ordering of the vertices of a DAG such that every edge $(u,v)$ goes from an earlier vertex $u$ to a later vertex $v$. It exists if and only if the graph is acyclic.
The directed graph $G^*$ on the same vertices that has an edge $(u,v)$ whenever $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $G$.
A directed graph $N=(G,s,t,c)$ with a source $s$, a sink $t$, and a non-negative capacity $c(u,v)$ on each edge.
The maximum amount of flow an edge is allowed to carry.
A function $f(u,v) \le c(u,v)$ that conserves flow at every vertex except $s$ and $t$. Its value $|f|$ is the net flow leaving the source $s$.
A partition of the vertices into $S \ni s$ and $T \ni t$. The capacity of the cut is the total capacity of the edges going from $S$ to $T$.
A cut of smallest capacity. By the max-flow/min-cut theorem, its capacity equals the value of the maximum flow.
The graph of remaining capacities under a flow $f$: each edge has a forward residual $c(u,v)-f(u,v)$ and a backward residual equal to $f(u,v)$.
A path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual graph along which extra flow can be pushed. Ford–Fulkerson repeats until none exists.
An edge whose flow equals its capacity, $f(u,v)=c(u,v)$; it has no forward residual capacity left.
A set of edges, no two of which share a vertex.
A matching to which no further edge can be added — but not necessarily one of the largest possible size.
A matching with the largest possible number of edges in the graph.
A matching that covers every vertex of the graph — each vertex is an endpoint of exactly one matching edge.
A set of vertices, no two of which are adjacent. It is the complement of a vertex cover: $\alpha(G)+\tau(G)=|V|$.
A set of vertices that touches every edge (each edge has at least one endpoint in the set). Minimum vertex cover is NP-hard; there is a factor-$2$ approximation.
The size of a largest **independent set** — a set of vertices with no edge between any two of them. Notation: $\alpha(G)$.
The size of a smallest **vertex cover** — a set of vertices touching every edge. Notation: $\eta(G)$.
The size of a largest **matching** — a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Notation: $\mu(G)$. Always $\mu(G) \le \eta(G)$; equality holds in bipartite graphs (König).
In every graph, a set $S$ is independent exactly when $V \setminus S$ is a vertex cover, so the maximum independent set and the minimum vertex cover always add up to $\lvert V\rvert$.

An undirected graph in which removing **any** single edge increases the number of connected components — equivalently, every edge is a bridge, equivalently the graph is a **forest**. A fragile graph can have several components, so it need not be a tree, and it can never contain a cycle.
A forest with $c$ connected components has exactly $\lvert V\rvert - c$ edges. A tree is the $c=1$ case with $\lvert V\rvert - 1$ edges.

The Travelling-Salesman Problem on a complete weighted graph whose weights satisfy the triangle inequality $w(u,v) \le w(u,x) + w(x,v)$. MST-doubling gives a $2$-approximation and Christofides a $1.5$-approximation; **general** TSP has no constant-factor approximation unless $P=NP$.
